sentences.text: King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: "Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: "The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: "Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: "The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Sarah Friar, OpenAI's chief financial officer, said AI had the potential to solve some of society's "hardest problems" - but agreed its growing capabilities raised questions about safety and "how we ensure it always serves people".
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: "We need to address those questions together," she said.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: "No one company or government can do that alone and I'm grateful to His Majesty for convening this discussion at such an important moment." Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".
sentences.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

sentences.text: The Bank of England has held interest rates at their current rate of 3.75% for the sixth time in a row but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies leading to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices and an uptick in inflation.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: But Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: The Bank also announced it was slowing its sales of UK government debt, prompting an easing in the UK's long-term borrowing costs.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: The Bank of England's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: Higher rates can help dampen inflationary pressures, while lower rates can help boost spending and investment.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years, with inflation hitting 3.1% in August .
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: On Thursday the Bank of England raised its forecast for inflation predicting it would be "slightly above 4%" at the start of next year.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: It warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January was "now expected to rise substantially further".
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: Other major central banks have increased rates to counteract higher prices.
sentences.article_title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

sentences.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to reform adult social care in England Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England.

sentences.text: An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target has been backed by Professor Sir Mike Richards, England's former national cancer director, and Baroness Louise Casey, who's leading a major review of adult social care.

sentences.text: In a report, Alzheimer's Society and the King's Trust said a "cancer-style revolution" was needed to improve dementia care, which they described as being "stuck in the 20th century".

sentences.text: In a speech at Alzheimer's Society conference on Thursday, Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report , external .
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: She said: "The report that the Alzheimer's Society published today on going on the journey that we've been on with cancer, with Alzheimer's and dementia, I think that's spot on." The minister said dementia had been "neglected for far too long".
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: McGovern said the government would "appoint a dementia tsar, backed with real expertise".
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: Currently there is no waiting-time target for dementia in England.
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: In contrast, the NHS sets waiting-time targets for cancer diagnosis and treatment.
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: He said setting such a target would require "political initiative" and extra funding.
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: "All of that is going to cost more money but remember the toll that this condition is taking at the moment, both on the people affected by dementia themselves and their relatives," the professor said.

sentences.text: The same proposal has been made by Baroness Casey.
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: In a letter to former Health Secretary Wes Streeting in March, she said the government should look at "how dementia can be put on a level playing field with other conditions, for example by setting national standards for dementia diagnosis, including an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target".
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: Speaking to the BBC, Baroness Casey said she agreed with the proposal to emulate cancer care.
sentences.article_title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

sentences.text: The Duke of Gloucester unveiled the freshly restored statue A statue of the 19th-century poet Lord Byron has been returned to Hyde Park, nearly 70 years after it was isolated on a traffic island when new roads were built through the area in the early 1960s.

sentences.text: The new virtual queuing pass has been welcomed by disability charities, and will be first introduced at Alton Towers A new virtual queuing system for visitors with accessibility needs to be introduced first at Alton Towers has been praised by charities.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: The upgraded ride access pass (Rap), to be in use later at other Merlin-run parks like Thorpe Park and Legoland Windsor Resort, enables queuing for rides via an app rather than in physical lines.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: The news follows a backlash in February when proposed changes led to visitors with conditions such as ADHD and autism being told they would not be able to use a physical Rap .
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: There will be no change to the eligibility criteria for the pass, available to those who have problems queuing for long periods because of a physical, emotional or learning need, Merlin says.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: Staffordshire-based Alton Towers will start accepting the revamped pass at the end of the year, with Merlin's other theme parks taking it on next year.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: During the row earlier in the year, families of children with additional needs told the BBC the restrictions would mean their children could not visit because of waiting in long queues, or sensory overload felt in crowded environments.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: Under the plan, visitors to places like Alton Towers, Chessington World of Adventures and Legoland Windsor over half-term who had "difficulty with crowds" would no longer have qualified.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: Merlin backtracked on the proposal days later following an online petition against it signed by more than 25,000, saying they had listened to the feedback and would pause the changes while considering other options.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: The changes would apply at parks including Chessington World of Adventures, Thorpe Park and Alton Towers However, disability experts, charities and partners such as Disability Rights UK, Scope, ADHD UK, and the National Autistic Society have welcomed the new virtual system, which they helped to shape.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: Lisa Myers, of the National Autistic Society, said she was pleased Merlin had consulted with autistic people and their families and that the Rap eligibility criteria would not change.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: "This is an example of an adaptation that can make a real difference to autistic people, enabling them to access facilities and venues," she said.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: Currently Merlin-run parks operate a reverse queue system for Rap holders, meaning they must pre-book a slot in advance to skip the queue for a ride, then wait before they can go on another.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: Under the new system, pass holders will wait for the same amount of time as those in physical queues and be notified on the app when they are near the front, meaning they can pass the time where they are most comfortable.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: Pass holders will then be helped to join a separate queue using a dedicated entrance.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: Merlin's chief operating officer, Rob Smith, said the firm had "listened carefully" to feedback from Rap users, charities and partners and believed the new system would "significantly improve visits".
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: "It's clear the current experience does not always provide the flexibility and comfort some guests need," he said.
sentences.article_title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised

sentences.text: "This new virtual queuing approach has been designed in response to that feedback." He added the firm wanted every guest to enjoy "memorable days out" and would continue to work closely with Rap users and advocacy group as the new system was rolled out.

sentences.text: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman OpenAI revealed six more incidents of unexpected or concerning behaviour by its intelligence (AI) models, and announced a plan for tracking and disclosing such incidents in the future.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Some of the previously unreported incidents included models concealing or fabricating information, the ChatGPT-maker said in a blog post on Wednesday.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: The boss of OpenAI Sam Altman said earlier this week: "The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this." AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days following warnings over the serious potential risks it poses to humans.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: In the blog, OpenAI detailed examples of its AI models misbehaving so they could achieve a task or succeed in a test.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: The incidents included the models generating instructions to get around restrictions imposed on them, hiding mistakes and fabricating information.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: The firm also announced a new system to track, investigate and disclose cases of models misbehaving, or "misalignment".
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Under the framework, developers will be able to flag incidents for review, with a new set of rules to decide whether the issue is disclosed publicly.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: "Because we believe in the value of transparency around misalignment, our new framework favors disclosure even when significance is uncertain," OpenAI said.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: OpenAI made headlines in July when it revealed that some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked Hugging Face, one of the world's largest hubs for sharing AI models, after it lost control of them during a security test.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf said at the time that the incident was "a wake-up call" for the industry.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Since then, the debate over AI safety concerns has escalated with AI researchers, technology industry executives and politicians weighing in.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Last week, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who left OpenAI rival Anthropic over concerns the tech could wipe out humanity, wrote about his resignation in a post that cited the dangers of AI and later went viral against the backdrop of growing safety concerns.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he thought the possibility of AI causing human extinction "within the next decade" was more than 10%.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark later told the BBC that a "kill switch" controlled by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Meanwhile, Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored, as the company has done before, though some have questioned the motivations behind this.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Amodei also said that any action to rein in AI should be done "without sacrificing commercial advantage".
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: But US President Donald Trump has said fears about the safety of AI are a "hoax" and criticised calls to have more guardrails in place for the fast-moving technology.

sentences.text: In a series of social media posts, the US president compared warnings about AI to the "Global Warming Scam" which, he said, was "being perpetrated by the Radical Left Dumocrats".
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: Trump also called himself "the Hoax Buster", likening concerns about the safety of the technology to what he called "the RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX".
sentences.article_title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents

sentences.text: The only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president, said Trump.

sentences.text: The Bank of England has kept UK interest rates unchanged at 3.75% for a sixth time in a row, keeping them at the lowest level since February 2023.
sentences.article_title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?

sentences.text: Before the US-Israeli war with Iran, rates had been expected to fall in 2026, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe, making cuts unlikely and rises a possibility.
sentences.article_title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?

sentences.text: Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people.
sentences.article_title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?

sentences.text: An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it.
sentences.article_title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?

sentences.text: The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings.
sentences.article_title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?

sentences.text: The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%.
sentences.article_title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?

sentences.text: This video can not be played Watch: New Yorkers, and LinkedIn's Nicole Leverich, share their networking tips For some, networking comes naturally but for others, the thought of approaching someone they don't know and trying to make a professional connection can fill them with dread.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Whether you're looking for your first job, trying to get ahead at work or hoping to change career, building a network can help you find opportunities and make connections.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Networking doesn't have to mean working a room at a formal event - it can happen in person over a coffee at work, through a chance conversation or online, through email and social media.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Just under half (44%) of Gen Z say not having the right network is the biggest barrier to landing an entry-level role, according to research from LinkedIn , external .
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Nicole Leverich, chief communications officer at LinkedIn, shares her top tips on how to network and we took the same question to city workers in New York to find out what has worked for them.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Everyone can start building their network online and "you'd be surprised how many connections you have once you connect with people you went to school with, former professors, people you met through summer jobs, family and friends," says Leverich.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Don't be discouraged if your network is small as "not having a network right now doesn't mean you'll never have a network", she says.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: And not having obvious industry contacts shouldn't put you off.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Leverich grew up in a small town in Oregon and moved to San Francisco after college without knowing anyone who worked in communications.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: In a message you should "reference something they've posted or establish some common ground".
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Make sure your request is "clear and specific" and something they can do in less than five minutes.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: And, most importantly, don't forget to say thank you.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "You'd be surprised by how many people are willing to help, but I get so few thank yous," she says.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "I'm not talking about anything excessive but just a 'thanks' makes you want to help next time." Networking can feel transactional, so to avoid that, try to build relationships before you need something from them, Leverich advises.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: If you know you want to work in a particular industry, "start finding people in that field a year or two before you're looking for a job".
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: When you reach out to them, think about what you can offer them in return.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "If you call me and say you want a job randomly, I'm much less likely to help than if you call and ask for five minutes of advice." You also don't have to start by messaging someone directly, she says.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Instead you could react to a post or drop a comment.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: In-person networking can be more daunting, particularly early in your career, but remember that at a networking event, everyone is there to talk.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: To begin a conversation, start with something simple like complimenting someone's outfit, introducing yourself and asking why they're there, Leverich advises.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Taylor Crow who works in sales says she's "fairly good" at networking as it was something she prioritised at university.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "I sent over 200 cold DMs (direct messages) on LinkedIn and reached out to people in the companies I wanted to work at while I was studying." She admits it was "so awkward" but it was something she had to do to land the job she wanted.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Her colleague Vicky Peterlin, 24, agrees.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "It's not about being good at networking but more about not being afraid to reach out to people.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "I had thoughts about how I'm not qualified to have these conversations but then you realise there are no rules and sending out emails and messages are free and easy.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "The worst that can happen is that they say no and that's ok." Katherine Leopold, a careers and employability tutor at Greenwich Business School, echoes this.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: She says the biggest hurdle is making the first move but if you don't take the step you are "ruling yourself out".
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: The number of applications that organisations are dealing with is "absolutely enormous" so try to meet employers in person and show them your total authentic story, she advises.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "Ensure you say to them, 'I have this skill, I have this piece of knowledge, so I'm confident that your team is stronger with me in it.'" Madison Brown works in tech partnerships, having previously worked in corporate jobs for 10 years.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: Madison says it's important to be authentic and intentional when reaching out to people He gets a lot of young people reaching out to him for career advice and opportunities, and says many of them could be much clearer in what they are looking for.
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: "There's nothing wrong with saying what your goal is or what you want to get out of this interaction." He adds that it's important to be yourself and "more doors will open if you are authentic".
sentences.article_title: I sent 200 LinkedIn messages and got a job: How to nail networking

sentences.text: A series of social media adverts for AI apps have been banned by a UK watchdog for promoting "the creation of sexually explicit content and objectification of women".
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said five ads uploaded to Meta platforms for AI companion and video generating apps had objectified and sexualised women, including through harmful gender stereotypes.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: One of the ads used sexualised images of a girl under 18 to promote an AI companion app - while others invited users to upload images of their "crush" and turn images into "sizzling" videos.

sentences.text: Meta had already removed the offending ads.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: But Nicky Baker of the ASA said such content had the potential "to cause real-world harm".

sentences.text: "We take a firm line on ads that are likely to cause serious or widespread offence and these ads are a clear example of why that matters," she said.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: "Encouraging and condoning the objectification of women and the creation of explicit content from people's images has the potential to cause real-world harm." The ASA also said many of the ads it banned had promoted the creation of sexually explicit content using real women's images without their consent.

sentences.text: It comes only months after the UK outlawed apps to create non-consensual deepfake nude imagery - sparked by outrage over X's chatbot Grok complying with requests to nudify images of women on the platform .

sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage pictured during the party's annual party conference earlier this month The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: The government is planning to tighten residency rules for people giving money to political parties, to ensure that those making significant donations live in the UK.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But it is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to £100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published, , external the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons , external that cap would be £100,000 per year.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: They have both now returned to the UK.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would be legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: "Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Ah, today, I pointed out.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: This video can not be played Farage: Donations to Reform '100% compliant with the law today' We don't know, because Reform won't tell us, precisely when the two men relocated to the UK.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Nor do we know, because the government hasn't decided yet, what relocating - residency - would look like legally.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Would it be being on the electoral roll at a UK address?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Would it be being resident in the UK for tax purposes?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: In other words the hurdles they plan, while still ill-defined, look like they might be quite high - and folk in government, publicly and privately, are leaning into making that point.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Farage picked a scrap with them in his interview with me, and the government is hitting back.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Do Delo and Harborne clear them, and if they don't, for how long could that delay Reform getting hold of their vast sums of money?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: The Reform UK leader has threatened that a Reform government would cut off party funding from the trades unions if the government went ahead with trying to limit his capacity to raise money from these two donors.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Labour received £5m from affiliated unions last year and £12m the year before, in 2024, the year of the last general election.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: So, there are loads of questions that tumble towards us after these donations.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Should there be a limit on the proportion of a party's funding that can come from one individual?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Should there be a limit on what donors based in the UK can give per year, as well as a cap on donations from Brits abroad?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: The General Secretary of the Unite union has suggested a domestic cap somewhere between £500,000 and £1m a year.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Some argue this would compel parties to find their funding via lots of small donations rather than fewer giant ones.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But it could also prompt some to call for state funding of political parties – ie taxpayers picking up the tab – which may not prove wildly popular.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Then there is the question of spending limits, in addition to donation limits, between elections on the top of the existing limits that do apply just before elections.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: If I am leaving you with the impression that these donations to Reform, and in particular their scale, are transforming the debates at Westminster about politics and money, well - they are.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: And yes, all of the political parties are aware of their own narrow, self interest in all of this - as well as their own sense of the wider good.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Around 400 million people now live in countries which have legalised assisted dying.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Spain and Austria are among those which have changed the law in recent years, with some allowing help to die for those who are not terminally ill.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Just last month, France adopted an 'aid in dying' law for adults with incurable conditions causing them unbearable pain.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: While most jurisdictions forbid medical help to die, assisted dying laws around the world vary.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Across the US, assisted dying - which some critics prefer to call assisted suicide - is legal in 13 out of 50 states, as well as in Washington DC.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Oregon was one of the first places in the world to offer help to die for some patients, in 1997, and so has nearly 30 years' experience.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It has become the model on which other US assisted dying laws have been framed.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In Oregon, assisted dying is open to terminally ill , external , mentally competent adults expected to die within six months - and must be signed off by two doctors.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Since 1997 , external , 5,520 people have received a prescription for a lethal dose of medication - with 3,691 deaths.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In a 2025 report , external , 61% of patients who ask for help to die had cancer, 14% had a neurological condition like motor neurone disease and 11% had heart disease.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Around one in three of those prescribed a lethal dose don’t go ahead with it.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Oregon is important for supporters of assisted dying in England and Wales as they point out it has remained restricted to terminally ill adults since its introduction.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: However, opponents say some of the rules have been relaxed.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: A residency requirement has been lifted, which means it is open to people from outside the state.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The number of assisted deaths has also risen substantially over the years.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Canada is the country often cited by opponents of assisted dying as an example of the so-called "slippery slope" - a place where assisted dying has been extended and made available to more people since it was first brought in.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Medical assistance in dying (Maid) , external was introduced in 2016, initially just for the terminally ill.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: This was amended in 2021 and extended to those experiencing "unbearable suffering" from an irreversible illness or disability.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It had been due to be extended to people with a mental illness but that is now on hold.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Critics say the more the law is widened, the more disabled and vulnerable people will be put at risk.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: There has also been a dramatic growth in the number of people using Maid.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Roughly one in every 20 deaths in Canada are now medically assisted , external , compared to about one in 100 in Oregon.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Across Europe, several countries have legalised assisted dying: Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain, Austria, Portugal and, most recently, France.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Eligibility criteria vary widely.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Some jurisdictions allow assisted dying for people who are not terminally ill, while others, including France, restrict it to adults with serious incurable illnesses nearing the end of life.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Portugal's law was approved in 2023 but is not yet in force because of court and regulatory delays.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In 2025, Tuscany became the first region of Italy to establish a legal process for medically assisted suicide.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Earlier rulings by the constitutional courts in both Italy and Germany removed criminal penalties for assisted suicide in certain circumstances.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The Netherlands and Belgium both legalised assisted dying more than 20 years ago for patients experiencing unbearable suffering from an incurable illness, including mental health issues.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It has since been extended to children - the only European countries to allow this.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Both allow euthanasia - or physician-assisted dying.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Spain and Austria legalised assisted dying for both terminal illness and intolerable suffering in 2021 and 2022, respectively.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In Austria, the drugs must be self-administered, whereas in Spain a medical professional can administer them.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In England, Wales and Scotland, parliament has so far rejected assisted dying proposals.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: But assisted dying has already been legalised in one part of the British Isles.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In July, Royal Assent was given to a bill in Jersey.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Unlike at Westminster and Holyrood, the legislation was introduced by the Jersey government, which says it will take about 18 months to set up the service.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The first assisted death could happen late next year.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: There will be a residency requirement of one year, in a bid to prevent so-called 'death tourism'.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The measure, which most sets apart the Jersey legislation from the rest of the British Isles, concerns the manner in which those eligible for an assisted death can end their lives.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Individuals will be able to choose to have a doctor administer a lethal dose intravenously, as happens in Spain, Canada, New Zealand and most of Australia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: This is, in effect, voluntary euthanasia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: It has become the preferred method of assisted dying in jurisdictions which allow this choice.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The laws proposed at Westminster, Holyrood and Tynwald - Isle of Man - all state that death must be by self-administration, which usually means the individual swallowing a lethal dose.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: The Isle of Man assisted dying bill was passed by Tynwald (the Manx parliament) in March last year.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: As a UK Crown Dependency - like Jersey - it could not become law until granted Royal Assent.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: This was declined earlier this year by the UK Ministry of Justice, but Tynwald has since passed an updated bill which has been sent back to the UK government for a second time.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: If Royal Assent is granted, the Isle of Man expects the service to be operational next year.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: There is a residency requirement of five years.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In the past few years voluntary assisted dying has become legal across most of Australia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Last month, the Northern Territory parliament became the last part of Australia to pass Voluntary Assisted Dying legislation.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In New Zealand, patients must be terminally ill and expected to die within six months.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: That is extended to 12 months for those with a neurodegenerative condition in much of Australia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In both countries, patients can self-administer the lethal medication.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: But it can also be administered by a doctor or nurse, usually via an intravenous injection.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: In South America, Uruguay passed a law in 2025 to permit assisted dying for adults with an incurable or terminal illness.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Across Latin America, Colombia, Ecuador and Cuba have decriminalised euthanasia.
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Additional reporting by Anthony Reuben and Gerry Georgieva
sentences.article_title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world

sentences.text: Sarah Mackay, known as @fitwsarah online, says her energy levels change through her cycle A woman points to a colour-coded grid dividing the menstrual cycle into four phases, each paired with a different list of exercises.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "When you're bleeding, you want to be doing steady-pace jogging, Pilates, barre, walking, resting," she tells viewers.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: This is one of thousands of videos on TikTok and Instagram suggesting that people change their workouts depending on where they are in their menstrual cycles - something known as 'cycle-syncing'.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: So-called cycle-syncing workout plans have surged in popularity online, with Google searches for the term rising 740% since 2022 and more than 55,000 TikTok videos now using the #cyclesyncing hashtag.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Most of the advice is shared by fitness and wellness creators rather than medical or research experts.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Kelly McNulty, a researcher at Leeds Beckett University specialising in menstrual cycles and exercise, says there is evidence that some women experience changes in symptoms, energy or perceived strength across their cycle.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: But that is different from evidence that all women should train in a particular way at a particular point, she tells the BBC, adding that these videos are "a trend based on marketing rather than any kind of research or evidence".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "There isn't any research to support that kind of phase-based prescription," she says.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: This video can not be played Should you sync your exercise routine with your period?
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: A key issue is that menstrual cycles are highly individual, McNulty adds - they can differ between women, and one woman's experience can also change from one cycle to the next.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: That makes the blanket advice often found on social media difficult to apply, she explains.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Many cycle-tracking apps and programmes are also designed around relatively regular menstrual cycles that are 21 to 35 days, which can make their recommendations less applicable to people with irregular periods, or those using hormonal contraception.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: She doesn't follow a prescriptive plan, she says, but instead makes changes intuitively.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "In my luteal phase I'll try and ease off in the training," she tells the BBC.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "In my follicular phase, I'm so energised, I feel like I can lift so much heavier.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: I like to try and get my long runs in." Burgoyne also welcomes the growing attention on women's health, and says that exercise and nutrition research has historically focused heavily on male bodies, with findings then often applied to women.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Sarah says she has sometimes hit personal records while on her period Fitness creator Sarah Mackay, known as @liftwsarah on Instagram and TikTok, has also noticed her energy, motivation, cramps and mood change through the month.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: But she deliberately avoids strict plans because, she says, "there are too many variables at play".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Some online plans advise women to avoid intense training during their period, she says, yet she has sometimes hit personal records while menstruating.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "The problem is not that the menstrual cycle is irrelevant," she says, but that "not everything is predictable".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Dr Faye Bate, a trained medical doctor and women's health expert, is also wary of advice suggesting all women should train differently according to their menstrual phase.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: "A one-size-fits-all model of 'you should be exercising this way in this phase and a different way in a different phase' shouldn't be advice that applies to all women," she says.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: She is concerned that repeatedly telling women they are likely to be weaker or less capable at particular points in their cycle could create a "nocebo" effect - where negative expectations themselves influence how someone feels or performs.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: McNulty tells the BBC that routinely easing off resistance training could also limit progress.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Strength training is particularly important for women, who face a higher risk of osteoporosis later in life.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: While cycle-syncing itself may not be backed by strong evidence, the experts we spoke to did suggest being "cycle-aware".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: McNulty says tracking your cycle can be a useful way to understand your own patterns, while Dr Bate also encourages women to become more familiar with how they feel at different points in the month.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Both welcome the fact that menstrual health is being discussed more openly, but say the focus should be on individual experience, rather than rigid, phase-based rules.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: In practice, that might mean having painkillers ready before your period, taking a rest day when symptoms are worse, or easing off a workout if you feel unusually fatigued.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: For Dr Bate, "the most important part is tuning in to how you feel".
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: In other words, use your cycle as information rather than a set of rules.
sentences.article_title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts

sentences.text: Have you ever slept next to a snoring partner and woken up feeling stressed, unfocused or forgetful the next day?
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: As snoring is relatively common, it is often left untreated and dismissed as a harmless irritation.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: But according to experts, sleeping next to a snorer could be impacting your health.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Snoring is caused by the vibration of the soft tissues in our upper airways during sleep, explains Dr Clare Simon, a dentist with a special interest in dental sleep medicine.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: About 40% of the UK adult population snores, with the issue affecting more men than women, says the British Snoring and Sleep Apnoea Association (BSSAA).
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: And 75% of people with a snoring partner say they have had their sleep impacted, according to a US survey by the Sleep Foundation.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Here's what you need to know about the impact on partners - and what you can do about it.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Prof Ama Johal, a consultant orthodontist and sleep expert at Aerox Health, explains that the partner of a snorer can become "so impacted upon that it's almost a last-ditch effort on their part to get up and go sleep in a separate room because they have to sleep".
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: He adds: "As humans we physically can't function without that necessity." Prof Ama Johal says many couples put up with the negative effects snoring for too long During the night, we cycle through different stages of sleep in repeating patterns, usually every 90 minutes.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: The deeper stages of this cycle are important for physical restoration.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: If sleep is frequently disrupted, you may spend less time in the restorative stages, meaning you can wake up feeling tired, even if you've spent a lot of time in bed, the BSSAA explains.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Your brain processes and stores information from the day during sleep.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Fragmented sleep - which can happen if you're waking up due to a snoring partner - can interrupt this process, impacting your focus and memory.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Disrupted sleep can also impact hormone regulation, which affects your energy levels and motivation.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: Sleep also plays a role in regulating the brain systems involved in stress and emotional response.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: When it is disrupted, these systems can become less balanced, which may make you feel more irritable and less able to cope with stress.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: This is something Meg Warren, 29, experienced when her former partner's snoring would keep her up.
sentences.article_title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health

sentences.text: She says: "Without fail, after a snoring-induced wake up I would feel on incredibly high alert." Meg, a charity media officer, would prod him throughout the night and try to coax him from his back to his side.

sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement).

sentences.text: Many also give users a "sleep score".
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "That's just been created by manufacturers." This video can not be played How sleep-tracking can make your sleep worse Hare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients.
sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: "I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says.

sentences.text: Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds.

One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct".

sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.article_title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse

sentences.text: As a period of extreme heat is forecast across the UK this week, UV levels are expected to be high in many areas.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Some exposure to UV is essential for our wellbeing, but too much is damaging and can cause skin cancer.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: UV radiation is emitted by the Sun and penetrates the Earth's atmosphere.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: It enables our skin to produce essential vitamin D, which is important for the function of bones, blood cells and our immune system.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: But too much UV can be harmful.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: It can lead to skin cancer by damaging DNA in skin cells.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: UV also plays a substantial role in skin ageing, contributing to wrinkles and loosened folds.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: It has also been linked to eye problems , external , including cataracts.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: "Every exposure to UV, especially every sunburn, increases our risk of skin cancer," says Prof Dorothy Bennett, from St George's, University of London.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: "Melanoma, the most dangerous skin cancer, is now the fifth commonest cancer in the UK." UK's hottest May day record broken for second day in a row How long will the heatwave last?

sentences.text: Why temperature records are being not only broken but smashed Levels of UV radiation vary throughout the day.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: The highest readings are in the four-hour period around "solar noon", when the sun is at its highest - usually from late morning to early afternoon.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: The UV Index (or UVI) is a measure of ultraviolet radiation used around the world.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Values start at zero and can rise above 10.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: The higher the number, the greater the potential for damage to the skin and eyes, and the less time it takes for harm to occur.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: In the UK, the UV index would typically be around 5-6 during the summer, with a maximum of 8 only in exceptional circumstances.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Countries close to the equator can experience very high UV levels in the middle of the day, throughout the year.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Nairobi in Kenya, for example, can have UV levels above 10 all year, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Majorca in Spain normally hits nine in June and July.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Appropriate sunscreen is essential.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Some sun protection is required when UK levels are medium (3-5) or high (6-7), the WHO says.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Extra sun protection is required when UV levels are very high (8-10) or extremely high (11+).
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: Children are more sensitive to UV radiation than adults, and therefore require additional protection at lower levels than adults.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: The NHS advises , external using sunscreen with an SPF factor of 30 or above and which offers at least 4-star UVA protection.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: It should be applied to all exposed skin, including the face, neck and ears - and head if you have thinning or no hair - ideally 30 minutes before you go out into the sun.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: As a guide, adults should aim to apply about six to eight teaspoons of sunscreen if covering the entire body.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: It should be reapplied every two hours, or sooner if you sweat a lot, have been in water, or after drying yourself with a towel.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: In addition, the NHS recommends: covering up with suitable clothing and wearing sunglasses spending time in the shade when the sun is strongest - between 11:00 and 15:00 from March to October in the UK What should you look for when choosing sunscreen?

sentences.text: "When you tan, ultraviolet light stimulates your skin cells to produce pigment to try and protect the DNA of skin cells - but that protection is minimal -  the equivalent of SP4.

sentences.text: "That is not much protection at all - so you can still burn very early," he warns.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: The amount of UV reaching your skin is not driven by the daily temperature.
sentences.article_title: What are UV levels and how can you protect yourself?

sentences.text: "Your skin can burn just as quickly whether it's 30C or 20C," warns BBC Weather's BBC Weather's Helen Willetts.

sentences.text: "Don't be caught out on cloudy days.
